q: Which mobile state belongs in a screen, and which must survive app termination?
a: Keep temporary presentation state with the screen; persist important user data and recoverable workflow state durably.
explanation: A recreated screen or process is not the same as a new user action. Define restoration requirements for navigation, drafts, and completed transactions rather than persisting every UI detail.
mistake: Keeping the only copy of an important draft in memory.
followups: Should a loading indicator be restored?

q: A mobile app shows a spinner forever when the network disappears. What should change?
a: Model explicit loading, failure, retry, and usable cached-data states, with a bounded request timeout.
explanation: Reconnect does not prove the earlier operation failed. Preserve input, distinguish retriable reads from writes, and show actionable feedback. Test airplane mode and interrupted responses.
mistake: Treating every network failure as an endless loading state.
followups: What if a write succeeded before disconnect?
When should cached data be shown?

q: Design a repository for a feed that can read cached data and refresh remotely.
a: Expose a consistent local source of truth and coordinate network refreshes separately from presentation logic.
explanation: Persist a successful refresh before publishing it when durability matters. Define freshness, empty versus unavailable data, pagination, and cancellation. Inject dependencies for deterministic failure tests.
mistake: Returning conflicting local and remote data without a defined ownership rule.
followups: What if only one page refreshes?

q: Memory rises after repeatedly opening and closing a mobile screen. What would you inspect?
a: Measure retained screens and resources, then inspect subscriptions, callbacks, images, and lifecycle ownership.
explanation: Use platform profiling tools and reproduce a bounded navigation loop. Clean up owned observers and avoid long-lived objects retaining short-lived UI. Compare retained memory after the screen should be gone.
mistake: Calling memory cleanup blindly without identifying retained owners.
followups: What if image caches explain the growth?

q: Two devices edit the same mobile record offline. Design the sync behavior.
a: Use stable identity, version-aware updates, durable pending changes, and a conflict policy visible to users when needed.
explanation: Track deletions explicitly and do not rely on device clocks alone. Retries must be idempotent. Test out-of-order delivery, duplicate sync, and interruptions before marking edits synchronized.
mistake: Using last-write-wins without defining whose clock or which data can be lost.
followups: What if a device stays offline for months?

q: App startup slowed after adding several SDKs. How would you respond?
a: Profile startup phases and main-thread work, then defer initialization that is not required for the first usable screen.
explanation: Separate cold startup from restoration and measure representative devices. Account for disk, class loading, network, and SDK callbacks. Verify deferred initialization does not lose necessary events.
mistake: Moving all work later without checking correctness.
rubric: Verify deferred work and device coverage
followups: Which SDKs truly need early startup?

q: How would you structure mobile feature teams around a shared app?

explanation: Measure build speed and coordination cost before and after changes. Prevent shared modules from becoming dumping grounds and provide compatibility and migration rules for consumers.

q: Plan a mobile rollout when users keep old app versions for months.
a: Maintain compatible backend and local-data evolution, use phased releases, and observe version-specific failures.
explanation: Store rollout and rollback differ from a server redeploy. Use carefully bounded feature controls, define minimum-version policy, and test old clients. A rollback may not undo an on-device migration.
mistake: Assuming every installed app upgrades when a server changes.
